title: Turning the Report Up and Down

scenes.tts: Why can the same touch feel fine one day and hurt the next?
scenes.visual: A forearm and a shirt sleeve. The question on screen.
scenes.narration: Why can the same touch feel fine one day and hurt the next?

scenes.tts: After a mild sunburn, a brushing shirt hurts. A shower that used to sting a little now hurts a great deal.
scenes.visual: The arm turns sunburned. The sleeve brushes it; then shower drops fall on it.
scenes.narration: After a mild sunburn, a brushing shirt hurts. A shower that used to sting a little now hurts a great deal.

scenes.tts: Pain from a normally harmless touch is allodynia. Greater pain from something already painful is hyperalgesia.
scenes.visual: Two labels: allodynia beside the shirt, hyperalgesia beside the shower.
scenes.narration: Pain from a normally harmless touch is allodynia. Greater pain from something already painful is hyperalgesia.

scenes.tts: Same stimulus, different report. Its size can be reset at three levels.
scenes.visual: A line from skin to brain with three dials: ending, dorsal horn, brainstem.
scenes.narration: Same stimulus, different report. Its size can be reset at three levels.

scenes.tts: First, the ending. Injured tissue releases mediators such as bradykinin, which sensitize nociceptors.
scenes.visual: Dial one turns up. Bradykinin and protons drift onto a nerve ending.
scenes.narration: First, the ending. Injured tissue releases mediators such as bradykinin, which sensitize nociceptors.

scenes.tts: Second, the dorsal horn. Here, touch can change pain.
scenes.visual: Dial two highlighted. Zoom into the dorsal horn.
scenes.narration: Second, the dorsal horn. Here, touch can change pain.

scenes.tts: Bang your shin and you rub it. Gentle rubbing mainly excites touch fibres, yet it hurts less.
scenes.visual: A shin being rubbed. Large touch fibres light up. Label: model assumption, nociceptor input held fixed.
scenes.narration: Bang your shin and you rub it. Gentle rubbing mainly excites touch fibres, yet it hurts less.

scenes.tts: In nineteen sixty-five, Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed a gate.
scenes.caption: In 1965, Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed a gate.
scenes.visual: Names on screen: Melzack and Wall, 1965. Gate control theory.
scenes.narration: In 1965, Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed a gate.

scenes.tts: Picture two cells. A transmission cell sends the signal up, excited by both touch and pain fibres.
scenes.visual: Simplified gate circuit: a large fibre and a small fibre both excite a transmission cell with an arrow pointing up.
scenes.narration: Picture two cells. A transmission cell sends the signal up, excited by both touch and pain fibres.

scenes.tts: An inhibitory interneuron damps that cell. Touch fibres excite the interneuron. Pain fibres suppress it.
scenes.visual: An inhibitory interneuron in the substantia gelatinosa joins the circuit: plus from the large fibre, minus from the small fibre.
scenes.narration: An inhibitory interneuron damps that cell. Touch fibres excite the interneuron. Pain fibres suppress it.

scenes.tts: So rubbing adds damping, and less signal goes up.
scenes.visual: Large-fibre activity rises; the interneuron brightens; the upward arrow thins.
scenes.narration: So rubbing adds damping, and less signal goes up.

scenes.tts: But touch also excites the transmission cell directly. Rubbing helps only if the added damping wins.
scenes.visual: The large fibre's two paths glow: plus straight to the transmission cell, minus through the interneuron. Caption: rubbing helps only if the added damping outweighs the direct excitation.
scenes.narration: But touch also excites the transmission cell directly. Rubbing helps only if the added damping wins.

scenes.tts: In their nineteen sixty-five diagram, the damping acted on the incoming fibres themselves. This circuit is a simplified version.
scenes.caption: In their 1965 diagram, the damping acted on the incoming fibres themselves. This circuit is a simplified version.
scenes.visual: Historical panel, Melzack and Wall 1965: the inhibitory cell acts on the incoming fibre terminals. A second panel is labelled simplified modern gating model.
scenes.narration: In their 1965 diagram, the damping acted on the incoming fibres themselves. This circuit is a simplified version.

scenes.tts: Now remove the inhibitory interneuron. What does a light touch do?
scenes.visual: The interneuron greys out. A light touch arrives on the large fibre. The question on screen.
scenes.narration: Now remove the inhibitory interneuron. What does a light touch do?

scenes.tts: Nothing damps touch now. Touch alone can drive the transmission cell, sending a signal up the pain line.
scenes.visual: The touch signal passes straight through; the upward arrow fills.
scenes.narration: Nothing damps touch now. Touch alone can drive the transmission cell, sending a signal up the pain line.

scenes.tts: In twenty fourteen, Duan and colleagues removed inhibitory neurons of the dynorphin lineage in mice.
scenes.caption: In 2014, Duan and colleagues removed inhibitory neurons of the dynorphin lineage in mice.
scenes.visual: Names on screen: Duan and colleagues, 2014. Dynorphin-lineage inhibitory neurons grey out in a mouse dorsal horn.
scenes.narration: In 2014, Duan and colleagues removed inhibitory neurons of the dynorphin lineage in mice.

scenes.tts: Now light touch evoked pain-like withdrawal. Touch input was driving a pain line.
scenes.visual: A mouse paw withdraws from a light touch. Label: a behavioural sign of mechanical allodynia.
scenes.narration: Now light touch evoked pain-like withdrawal. Touch input was driving a pain line.

scenes.tts: That tests one form of spinal gating in mice, not the nineteen sixty-five diagram as drawn.
scenes.caption: That tests one form of spinal gating in mice, not the 1965 diagram as drawn.
scenes.visual: Caption: one form of spinal gating, in mice. Not proof of the 1965 diagram.
scenes.narration: That tests one form of spinal gating in mice, not the 1965 diagram as drawn.

scenes.tts: Third, the brainstem. It projects down to the dorsal horn, and can turn its signals up or down.
scenes.visual: Dial three highlighted. Periaqueductal gray to rostral ventromedial medulla to dorsal horn.
scenes.narration: Third, the brainstem. It projects down to the dorsal horn, and can turn its signals up or down.

scenes.tts: In rodents, one group of cells, called on cells, bursts just before a withdrawal from heat. Another group, called off cells, pauses just before it.
scenes.caption: In rodents, one group of cells, called ON cells, bursts just before a withdrawal from heat. Another group, called OFF cells, pauses just before it.
scenes.visual: Spike rasters around a withdrawal: ON cells fire at a background rate, then burst just before it; OFF cells pause.
scenes.narration: In rodents, one group of cells, called ON cells, bursts just before a withdrawal from heat. Another group, called OFF cells, pauses just before it.

scenes.tts: Off cells suppress pain-related processing, and on cells facilitate it. Control runs both ways.
scenes.caption: OFF cells suppress pain-related processing, and ON cells facilitate it. Control runs both ways.
scenes.visual: Two arrows from the brainstem to the dorsal horn: OFF cells, turn down; ON cells, turn up.
scenes.narration: OFF cells suppress pain-related processing, and ON cells facilitate it. Control runs both ways.

scenes.tts: A withdrawing paw is indirect evidence about pain. By itself, it does not show what the animal feels.
scenes.visual: Two labels: nociception (neural encoding) and pain (an experience). A paw withdrawal sits under nociception, with a dotted arrow to pain.
scenes.narration: A withdrawing paw is indirect evidence about pain. By itself, it does not show what the animal feels.

scenes.tts: A nociceptor's firing is a report. Pain is what the nervous system makes of it.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the report can be turned up or down at the ending, the dorsal horn and the brainstem.
scenes.narration: A nociceptor's firing is a report. Pain is what the nervous system makes of it.
